newsitem.title: INDIA: India asks U.S. to spell out trade concerns.
newsitem.headline: India asks U.S. to spell out trade concerns.

text.p: India, facing international pressure to open its market, has asked the United States to list priority sectors in which New Delhi could roll back trade barriers, a senior U.S. trade official said on Wednesday.
Deputy U.S. Trade Representative Jeffrey Lang told Reuters in an interview he discussed trade barriers to consumer goods during two days of talks with Indian counterparts.

"We have been invited to specify exactly what sectors are of interest to us and what time scales are of interest to us," he said. "We will schedule a discussion on that probably in Washington in mid-December to present our views to the Indian side."
In January, India must spell out its plans for lowering barriers to imports.
Although New Delhi launched a trade liberalisation programme in 1991, it has been reluctant to open its markets for electronic equipment and goods like refrigerators.
Lang said he hoped the discussions between Washington and Delhi would help India satisfy international trading partners at a meeting set for mid-January in Geneva.
Lang said the United States would spell out its views over India's trade barriers.
Lang said the United States and India could join to make quick progress in increasing trade in information technology.
He also urged India to offer greater opportunities to foreign bidders in its government procurement process.

"Given the huge size of government procurement in the United States and importance of government here in India and in other developing countries, the idea of exchanging concessions, in terms of access to government procurement, is clearly a mutual benefit to both sides," Lang said.
Under a World Trade Organisation agreement, governments are supposed to ensure a level playing field for foreign companies interested in bidding for state contracts.
Last month India said it would prefer that developing nations be able to retain the option of adhering to the WTO agreement and not be forced to join.
Lang said India could make a "good first step" by setting clear-cut rules and following transparent procedures in the awarding of such contracts.
He also urged India to adopt laws protecting domestic and foreign patent-holders from unfair competition.
